utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are sorry about that mishap and the delay. Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask a clarification from the Chamber. We spoke about my need to depart to Belgrade on the 22nd due to my passport problems. According to the latest schedule, there is a trial scheduled for the 27th. Did you decide that there was going to be a session on that day or not? I'm -- this is important for me because, since I lost my passport, first I need to go back to Belgrade to declare it lost, which makes the procedure of issuing a new passport much complicated. After that, I need to get a visa. Hence, I am afraid that I won't be able to return on the 27th. That's why I raise this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the last time we talked about that issue, we did say that we will not be sitting on the 27th and that you could be away on that day. If according to the latest schedule that day still says we are sitting, I'm sure it must be a mistake. You can take it that we will not be sitting. I think that that's what we agreed on that day. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Babic. Can you understand me clearly in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Babic, can we remind you that you are still bound by the declaration that you took to tell the truth and nothing else but the truth. Thank you very much, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, can you understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Again, if at any time you can't understand me in a language that you understand, or if you don't understand my question, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yesterday when we finished, you were telling us that Milan Martic was appointed on the 27th of June 1991 to the position Minister of Interior after having been formally appointed for a short period of time as Minister of Defence. After Mr. Martic became -- was formally appointed to Minister of Interior I should say who became the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since no one was appointed Minister of Defence at the time, as the Prime Minister, for a while I performed those tasks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until that fall, when the new minister was appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the new minister that was appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel Milan Tarbuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall when he was appointed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps in November. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yesterday you -- we also talked about how on the 1st of August 1991 there was a decision passed in the SAO Krajina to apply the Law of Internal Affairs of Serbia to the SAO Krajina and we looked at and put into evidence that Law of Internal Affairs of Serbia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall how long that law was in effect in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That law was in effect until December 1991; more or less it was copied and adopted as one of the laws of the SAO Krajina. It was Milosevic's recommendation that we do not -- we do not declare the Serbian laws in Krajina per se but that we copy them and then put them into force as the laws of the SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did he make that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He recommended that by that summer, late summer or beginning of fall 1991, when we started putting into force Serbian laws in our territory, but those at the time were not our own laws. He said that we shouldn't state that in such an open manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why he stated that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the obvious links with Serbia shouldn't be so obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why not? Why shouldn't they be obvious?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He envisaged a concept of creating a new state which would be a reduced Yugoslavia, including the Serbs in all of the former republics, in a way that we should act covertly and take over the territories, militarily speaking, wherever the Serb people lived, and he had the idea of creating this new state in a rather passive way or slowly so that it wouldn't be seen as a Serb expansion but in simply putting together a new Yugoslavia in its reduced forms, and this can be seen from some of the laws put into force on the 1st of April, such as the one by which we attempted to join SAO Krajina with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask you more questions about that later, but I'll just ask you this now. Why, in your understanding, did this have to be done covertly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that the international community wouldn't accuse Serbia for destroying Yugoslavia and trying to create Greater Serbia, but rather to have things done covertly in terms of what was done by Milosevic from Serbia and the Serbs who supported his concept in creating this new state, as well as so that Serbia wouldn't be blamed by the international community for the war and the break-up of Yugoslavia, to cover its real role.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what was -- if there was a covert strategy, what was the public position? What was publicly stated?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The public strategy began being voiced as of the summer of 1990, by putting forward the policies of Milosevic and the Socialist Party, presenting their wish to retain the firm type of federation and to preserve the right on self-determination up to secession, and he advocated such idea with the federal bodies by which republics and municipalities were to voice their opinion on the matter. That was the public view, the right to self-determination, up to secession, in those areas where a certain people was in majority. The covert strategy, however, was creating paramilitary forces, first in Croatia and then elsewhere, then to provoke incidents and to try and include the JNA into the events, first to separate the warring parties and then to deploy the JNA in those territories that were envisaged as the future Serb state and to later on retain the de facto situation that was supposed to have been recognised at a later stage by the international community.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We will come back to there topic, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Chamber, the decision that the witness referred to with respect to the creation of the Law of Internal Affairs in the SAO Krajina is actually contained in the 89(F) statement and it's at tab 44.1 and 44.2, just for future reference on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you testified yesterday that in May of 1991, it was your initiative to put Milan Martic into the position of Minister of Defence and that your purpose was to weaken him. And you gave some explanations and reasons for that. At the beginning of August of 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- did you continue to try to get control over the Ministry of the Interior in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of August, that is the same day when Mr. Martic suggested adopting the Law on Internal Affairs, I suggested that we declare a decision on the disbanding of the State Security Services in Krajina to be declared null and void, and that was an attempt to establish government control over the ministry and the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at 65 ter Exhibit 106? Could we scroll down, please? Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the decision that was published in the Official Gazette of the Krajina and it was put into force by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, what decision is this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The title is Decision to Abolish the State Security Service on the Territory of the Serbian Krajina promulgated by the government of the SAO Krajina on its session on the 1st of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was the head of the state security or DB in the SAO Krajina at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Orlovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you initiate this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I initiated this decision not only to replace Dusan Orlovic but it was envisaged in a way to abolish overall activities of the State Security Service within the territory of the SAO Krajina. It wasn't only the State Security Service of Krajina headed by Dusan Orlovic but rather it was the state security of Serbia being active in the territory of Krajina. That's the way the decision was formulated in such manner. It was my way to try to do away with the legitimacy of their activities in Krajina and to try to deny and remove their control over the Ministry of Defence. Dusan Orlovic personified the service but close to him there were always Frenki Simatovic and some other people in Krajina and Jovica Stanisic himself who often spent his time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What activities on the part of the state security in the SAO Krajina were you concerned about at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They basically managed the Krajina Police, the volunteers units and units that were directly under their command. They were provoking and trying to establish their own system of control and power that wasn't controlled by the government, and it was impossible to control that politically. This included provoking at the front lines, provoking the non-Serb populations as well as provoking all-out conflict. Put in a very few words, they had an overall control of all of the events at that time in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, how would they provoke the front line -- at the front lines and provoke the non-Serb populations and provoke all-out conflict? Specifically what did they do to provoke?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their activities began in April 1991. At first, they promoted discriminatory policies against Croats. Only Croatian houses were searched and only Croatians were searched for weapons. Then they were provoking in the areas in contact with the Croatian settlements and areas, in particular the settlements controlled by the Republic of Croatia. They tried to provoke incidents and to bring the JNA into the events, which at the time was still being the -- a buffer zone between the warring parties and at the later stage they became militarily active themselves as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that occur, the later stage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They began with combat activities as of end of June 1991, throughout the summer, and onwards throughout August and September and throughout the conflict, since this decision took no effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you talk about -- talked about these provocations you talked about Croatian houses were searched and Croatians searched for weapons and then you referred to Croatian settlements. Where are these settlements that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The territory of Knin in April and May, in Potkonje, and Kninsko Polje and Vrpolje were the settlements searched, and those activities incited some press communiques made by the ministry and the then secretary, Mr. Martic, and his aides openly discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are those settlements that you referred to all within the municipality of Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You -- let's go back to this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And actually could it be moved into evidence, please? 65 ter 106?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document 65 ter 106 is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 187, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, this decision of August 1st 1991 to disband the State Security Service in the SAO Krajina, was it successful?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But it created a lot of turmoil in Knin at the time and caused problems to me personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe on the same day, and on the following day, the head of the DBA in Serbia, Jovica Stanisic, showed up in Knin and he addressed me in a very strict manner asking me, well, what have you done? And I started to explain in a way that we were going to set up a separate national security agency and that perhaps it would be a good idea for him to assist us in that as an experienced expert in these matters at some point in the future, and in a way I was both justifying myself and on the other hand I was trying to escape from this pressure that he was putting me under but he only scowled really and went off. In other words, he found that unacceptable. On the next day conflicts broke out with his staff, Stanisic's staff, Captain Dragan and Frenki who were in Knin. The occasion was the markings of the TO that were being placed where captain Dragan's units were located, and that led to a further increase of tensions between myself and all of them. If you would like me to give you a description of the events that followed, I could do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me first ask to bring up 65 ter Exhibit 108.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for clarification of the Bench, "the tensions between myself and all of them," who were the "all of them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stanisic, Simatovic, and Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you see on your screen a document dated the 2nd of August 1991?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a decree on the insignia worn by the members of the armed forces, the Territorial Defence and special purpose units of the SAO Krajina, and it was passed by the president of the government, the head of government of the SAO Krajina on the 2nd of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose was for the armed forces in Krajina to be given the relevant insignia as it is enshrined in all the international standards, in order to fully fit in within a legal system which was being created on the territory of the SAO Krajina. And in order for to us have a unified Defence system which was in the making.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could scroll down to section 4 of the document, could you read that section, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All members of the armed forces shall wear the same badge in their caps as the members of the armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you read it again? Because I think there was a problem with the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, yes, number 4.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Members of the police shall wear the same badge on their caps as members of the armed forces."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 188, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'm going to ask you to explain for us what happened as a result of this decision but I want to show you two other decisions first before we do that. Could we see 65 ter Exhibit number 105, which is also Exhibit 31 in evidence? Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the decision about the application of the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia on the territory of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was passed by the government of the SAO Krajina on the occasion of the second session held on the 2nd of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why was this passed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to create a legal basis for the setting up and the unifying of all the TO units in order to have uniform in a single united system of the armed forces in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is already in evidence so I won't move it into evidence. Could we see -- well, before we do that, could we look at number 6 on this document? I'm going to read it and ask you could comment on it. "The president of the government of Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina is by his position commander of Territorial Defence, i.e., armed forces of Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina." Did that refer to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since in the original law there is no reference to the head of government but the president of the republic as is the case in Serbia. And in Krajina, we had different situation so those powers according to the decree in Krajina would have referred to the head of government, that is to say myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you trying to get control through this decision over the armed forces of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you successful?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look now at 65 ter Exhibit 107, please? Could that be -- I think it's a little hard to read. I wonder -- Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It is the information about the passing of the decision on the application of the Law of Defence on the Republic of Serbia on the SAO Krajina and it is addressed to, as you can see, presidents of municipal assemblies, commanders of municipal territory defence on the territory of the SAO Krajina, and the date is 2nd of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is it from you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please? The -- that's good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second paragraph I'll read it out, "In accordance with the said law, the Prime Minister of the SAO Krajina, Dr. Milan Babic, is commander of all armed forces in the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina." Is this a follow-up to the previous document that we saw?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is just a document including the information about the previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 189, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to go back now to the decision with respect to the insignia that's Exhibit number 188, from the 2nd of August 1991. You started to explain what happened as a result of that decision. Could you tell us what the result of that was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The result was that I encountered a great deal of opposition on the part of the State Security Service and the police force that was under their control at the time, and also I ran into a great deal of opposition and resistance on the part of the commander and the Chief of Staff of the 9th Drina Corps. Following the decision on the insignia --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you for a moment. The commander and the Chief of Staff of which corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Knin Corps --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was the commander and Chief of Staff of the 9th Knin corps?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, it was JNA Spiro Nikovic and Lieutenant Ratko Mladic was the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about that first. Did you -- what kind of resistance did you get or opposition did you get from them? How did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean within the police force or the JNA? Which --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, let's start with the JNA. What happened with the JNA with respect to this decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff of the 9th Knin corps, Colonel Ratko Mladic, invited me to the office of the corps commander at their command in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where was that located?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the centre of town, in the centre of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us with respect to the fortress which you've already talked about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just below the fortress, about 100 metres below.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was received by Colonel Mladic who was absolutely furious. He was shouting that they would not tolerate any separatist politicians, that they would not acknowledge any of that and that everyone had to be under the same command and wearing the same insignia, and he went to another office and he brought a red star and very angrily he banged it on the table, and he said, "Go on, take that. That's the common insignia." And I just shrugged, and I took the thing, put it in my pocket, and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was it that he gave you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The red five-pointed star which was the insignia of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the reaction now from the state security and the police? What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said to some of the staff, who were in my building at the town hall to create this insignia and to place it on the building at the Knin fort, where the command headed by Captain Dragan was, and also the units which were under the command of the DB. They made the sign and they took it up there, but Captain Dragan said that he wouldn't stand for it, and he said something disparaging about myself, and he sent the man back. And then after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I'm sorry to interrupt you but can you remind us again who Captain Dragan was and what position he held at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Dragan was Dragan Vasiljkovic and he was known under the name Captain Dragan in Knin. He was an employee of the State Security Service of Serbia and his role was training of special police units in Krajina, as well as the volunteer groups at Golubic camp and he was a commander of a special unit which was under the direct control of the State Security Service of Serbia and at the time that unit was stationed in Knin, and his command post was at the Knin fort at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That unit that he directly commanded, what was it called? Did it have a name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, they were called "Knindzas."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Captain Dragan and the Knindzas, were they under a command, were they under anybody's command at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were under the command of Frank Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you when you were telling us that the -- you sent the man up with the insignia and then he came back and what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't just send the guy back but he also chased away a whole unit of Territorial Defence from the municipality of Knin, people who were guarding the water supply and the reservoirs that were placed around the fortress, just above and just below the fortress walls. And having heard of what happened, I myself went up to the fort to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened then, when you went up there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at the time when Captain Dragan was holding meeting with this unit in the building of the business club. I didn't know that the unit was there at the time so I entered the building, believing that he must be there alone or maybe accompanied with a couple of more people but whether I entered the meeting room I was rather surprised. There were between 30 and 60 people there, uniformed men, his entire unit, and he was sitting at the top table, and since I went in, I continued bravely on my way and I sat on the only empty chair which was next to Captain Dragan and I was later told that Frenki was sitting there before my arrival but whether he heard that I was on my way, he slipped off and hid in the adjoining room. Nobody addressed me. Nobody -- I addressed no one. I just sat there and I heard the end of Captain Dragan's speech, delivered to his unit. He said that politicians are to blame for his departure, and that -- and he told his men that they shouldn't worry about his departure, that he was leaving them in the hands of Frenki. That was the end of his speech. Thereupon everybody got up. Nobody addressed me in any way, and they lined up in front of the building and I went out of the building together with a driver, I think, and maybe there was somebody else with me, and I hurried to the part of Golubic where the buildings housing the municipal offices were situated and there was the second of the executive council of the municipality who had his office there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, let me just ask you a few questions about what you've just told us. First of all, do you know approximately what date this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened immediately after the 2nd of August, around about that time. Maybe even on the same day or a day or two later, I can't remember. Perhaps even on the same day or the very next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've referred a number of times to Frenki and just so our record is clear, it would are you referring to when you refer to Frenki?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's Franko Simatovic. He was known in Knin as Frenki. He was an employee of the State Security Service of Serbia and he was the chief of one of its departments, I think the second administration. That's what Milosevic told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did Milosevic tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around the 25th or the 26th of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You told us earlier that Captain Dragan was commanded by Frenki Simatovic. How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he said that he was leaving the unit to him, under his direct control, that's one source of information, and my other source of information was when I saw Frenki in May in the training camp at Golubic where he was acting as the host. That's where Captain Dragan was training men. Also, Jovica Stanisic told me that they were paying Captain Dragan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did Jovica Stanisic tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In mid-August, after these events that I've started to describe in Belgrade. In August 1991, after Captain Dragan left and after I asked Milosevic to remove Frenki from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know why -- you told us about the speech that Captain Dragan made but -- and about the fact that he was leaving, but do you know why he left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that he responded too openly and too vehemently. I think that was the reason. The state security wanted to calm the situation down so they sacrificed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you mean he responded too openly and to vehemently? To what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my decisions, and to the setting up of the system of Territorial Defence and the placing of all forces under a unified Territorial Defence system, and under the control of the government of the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say the state security wanted to calm the situation down so they sacrificed him, are you talking about the state security of the SAO Krajina or the state security of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The state security of Serbia. They were its chief protagonists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How far is Golubic from Knin approximately?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it's of assistance to the Chamber on page 25 of the atlas, which is in evidence though I don't have at my fingertips the number - it's page 25 - there is a map which shows both Knin and Golubic in the lower right. It's Exhibit 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you told us that you -- I interrupted you when you were telling us that you had left Knin and you went to Golubic. What happened there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Golubic to tell the secretary of the executive council of Knin municipality that they should not allow Captain Dragan to disband them. However, as I was on my way to Golubic, I was followed by members of Captain Dragan's unit. I didn't even notice them following me right away. It was only when I arrived at the place where this man called Strbac was supposed to be the members of the unit were already entering the village and shouting out to each other, setting up checkpoints. They were shouting, "Go there. You hold this point. You go to that house." I quickly went to hide in the pine woods and they entered the little house and they were yelling, "Who is our man? Who do we have to kill?" That was enough for me to look for a way out right away. I had worked as a dentist in the surgery and I knew about a side entrance leading into the fields, and I used that to escape and to flee to the village of Padzanej [phoen]. From there I called my family and told them to leave town, to go away from Knin. I spent the night there and in the morning I called Slobodan Milosevic and asked him to withdraw Franko Simatovic from the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he would.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it did. Either he withdrew him or Frenki went off somewhere and hid but at any rate he wasn't seen in Knin any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he ever return?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, in September. I know that. Certainly after Milosevic said, and I have started to speak about it, he called me to Belgrade, he told me that Frenki was a good guy, that he was getting complaints about him. Milosevic said to him that some of his men were complaining about him appointing a Croat as chief of the second administration. But he said that he was a good guy, that his father had been after the Ustasha, and that he should be sent back to the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was I think on the 26th of August 1991. On the day the JNA attacked Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you -- do you know -- well you said that Frenki returned in September. How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him myself, and I heard about his activities around Lovinac. I was told that his base was in Korenica as of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where is Lovinac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lovinac is a Croatian village in Gracac municipality in Lika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said you heard about his activities in Lovinac. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that together with Milan Martic and David Rastovic, and with a mortar platoon from Lapac he had fired at Lovinac, at the police station and at the village itself. I heard from him after these events, I heard him bragging that they had razed it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was bragging? You said "him." Who was "him"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you hear that? When did you hear him bragging?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September, after the events around Lovinac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you hear him bragging?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a restaurant at the entrance to the Knin fortress.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Aside from what you heard Frenki say about this event, do you know what happened at Lovinac, yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a report about these events and also I heard people from Gracac talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you hear in this report and from these people from Gracac talking about? What did you hear had happened in Lovinac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were saying that Martic, Frenki, and Rastovic were carrying out target practice with mortars, allegedly they were firing at the police station but they kept missing and people were laughing at them because they were shooting at the village instead, but they said it all counts as a hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You mentioned before when you were describing going to Golubic that you -- you mentioned the name Strbac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretary of the executive council of Knin municipality, who was a reservist in a TO unit which was supposed to be guarding the location for civilian structures of Knin municipality in case of need. He was supposed to be there but I didn't find him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's his first name?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to Exhibit 31 and Exhibit 189. Exhibit 31 was the 1st of August 1991 decision applying the Law of Defence of Serbia to the SAO Krajina, and Exhibit 189 was a communication sent by you on the 2nd of August 1991, to presidents of municipalities stating that you were the commander of all armed forces in the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document we have is on screen, is it already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that's in fact 189.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that 189? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think I asked you but just to get back on to this topic, through these decisions, were you trying to get control of the armed forces including the TO in the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why were you trying to get -- you've already told us why you were trying to get control over the police. Why were you trying to get control over the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two reasons, one general and one personal. The general reason was that there was a need to set up a system based on law. It should be well known who was responsible for what and what their tasks were. My personal reason was that I was the highest ranking and most responsible politician in the Krajina but I had no power. I felt that this might be something I could rely on in implementing my policy in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you succeed in getting control over the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long after these events, and during these events that I've been describing, the enactment of the laws and the conflict with the state security, Milosevic said that Martic should be appointed commander of the TO. That was one thing. Another thing was the influence of the JNA and the control of the Secretariat for National Defence by the federal organs and the JNA. Real control over the Territorial Defence was wielded by Mr. Martic as the commander of the Territorial Defence. I did not fully comply with Milosevic's order to have him appointed commander, but in fact, he carried out this duty until the 30th of September 199.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until 30th of September of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Martic -- Mr. Babic, when did Mr. Milosevic say to you that Mr. Martic should be appointed commander of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime at the beginning of August, before the 8th of August. I'm not sure exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where or how did that conversation occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a visual image of it in my memory. It was either a telephone message or a message sent through someone. I don't recall the meeting. I do, however, recall the meeting when Martic was in Belgrade to see Milosevic about this issue. That sticks in my memory much more.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in mid-August, between the 8th and the 18th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the first communication, whether it was telephone or message sent through somebody, did you in fact appoint Milan Martic as the commander of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appointed Milan Martic deputy commander of the Territorial Defence, trying to put him under government control in that way, and not have him become independent of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit 112 which is Exhibit 37 in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the order on the appointment of the deputy commander of the Territorial Defence or the armed forces of the Krajina SAO, which was issued on the 8th of August 1991 by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's Mr. Martic who is appointed as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, after -- just to be clear, after he was appointed deputy commander did he continue to hold the position of Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did Mr. Martic react, if you know, to being appointed as deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely because I don't think I had any contacts with him until we had that meeting in Milosevic's office. I thought that he was getting information from Milosevic and through his people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Tell us now about that meeting in Milosevic's office. How did it occur and who was present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was invited to come to Milosevic's office. I arrived there, and when I arrived Mr. Martic was already there. That was my first meeting with Mr. Martic, in Milosevic's office. The meeting lasted for quite a long time, an hour or two, perhaps two hours, but it boiled down to one thing: Milosevic persistently kept repeating that Mile should be the commander of the Territorial Defence, that Martic should be the commander of the Territorial Defence, that Martic should be the commander of the Territorial Defence, in the presence of Martic. Martic was smiling and nodding to show his approval. I don't even remember him saying anything. I kept explaining persistently that Mr. Martic was not qualified to hold that position, that this was something that a general of the army should do, and that I, as Prime Minister, was not in command of the armed forces. This required a professional soldier. That was my defence. That was what I said to Milosevic. The meeting, however, ended in the same way it had begun. I kept repeating my standpoint. Milosevic kept demanding the appointment and Martic kept nodding his approval. And then we parted. It was an exhausting meeting. It went on for a long time. And things were left at that. Martic moved to the command post in the Knin fortress and until the 30th of September he actually was the commander of the Territorial Defence, awaiting his formal appointment to that post. On the 30th of September, a general was appointed to that post, with the approval of Milosevic, and pursuant to his decision, and Mr. Martic then demonstratively left that command post and moved to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, it's time for a break but just for the purposes of the record I just want to clarify one thing in your answer. You said that was -- at the beginning of your answer you said "that was my first meeting with Mr. Martic in Milosevic's office." Just to be clear, was that your first meeting with Mr. Martic or your first meeting with Mr. Martic in Milosevic's office?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's when I saw and met Mr. Martic for the first time in Milosevic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The Court will take an adjournment, and we'll come back at 4.00 this afternoon. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, before the break, you said that Mr. Martic, in August and September, in fact, carried out the duties of the commander of the TO in the SAO Krajina. What did -- can you be more specific? What kinds of duties? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had very few contacts with him during that period. What I do know as to his activities is the following. I know he cooperated with the command of the 9th corps concerning the engagement of their units for combat activities. I also know that he went to Kostajnica to coordinate activities around Kostajnica and I know that he was arming the zone staff of the TO at Kordun at the time, as TO commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you knew all of these things? These three different things that you've just recounted?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had good insight in all three. After his appointment, I was at the fortress and I wanted to see what the situation was after Captain Dragan departed. When I came there, between the 15th and the 18th of August, 1991, I found Mr. Martic in the office, together with Lieutenant Colonel or Colonel Zdravko Tolimir, who was chief of security of the Knin corps. They were discussing something intimately but they interrupted their discussion after my arrival. A few days after that, Mr. Martic issued an ultimatum to the police station and the inhabitants of Kijevo and from some of the people who were with the JNA at the time I heard that people from the JNA dictated that letter, put that letter together, to him, but I didn't correlate his meeting with Tolimir at the time, perhaps later. Next time I saw him was in -- after Mr. Vukovic assumed command of this 9th Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the exact date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was invited to come and meet the new commander and Mr. Martic was invited as well, as well as the commander of corps, the then Colonel Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's the date of that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, sometime in September 1991. That is the same day or the next day after General Vukovic arrived in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovic asked Martic to brief him on the deployment of the units, and how they coordinate with the JNA units in the area. He was explaining something on the map, it was unmarked, and General Vukovic asked Mladic to clarify the situation. Mladic was also pointing at some things on the map throughout the area of Northern Dalmatia. They were naming troops and units and General Vukovic was quite astonished. He said, "Where is my corps? I want to see the operations map until this evening and I want to receive a full report." That's what he said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what did Mr. Martic do in that meeting? Did he brief on the deployment of the units?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, General Vukovic asked him to brief him on the deployment of his units, that's what he said, his units, and he gave him a marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Martic do? What did he --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was pointing at some things on the map, more or less. He was looking for certain locations. He was moving about the map, trying to find locations. He had difficulty with some of them. And the general became impatient. He said, "Mladic, you clarify it for me." Since Mladic seemed quite lost as well, the general interrupted the conversation. The map was not marked in any way. It was empty, blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when Mr. Martic started to talk about his units, what units was he talking about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't specify their names. He just said that "our units follow your tanks." That's the sentence he uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you understand him to mean by that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The witness previously explained that Mr. Martic did not specify anything, and now we are asking the witness to make conclusions and to speculate but what is it you make conclusions about if Mr. Martic did not specify any units? Then these are just witnesses' assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is what did he make of that unspecified statement. He can give an interpretation to that statement, can't he? Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, when Mr. Martic said, "Our units follow your tanks," what did you understand him to mean by that, if anything?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two types of units, TO units, where they were formed, and the special police units. Those are the only types of units he could have had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office of the commander of the 9th Corps in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, you told us about that meeting in response to an earlier question which was to tell us how you knew about the various ways that Mr. Martic was exercising command and you gave three examples, cooperating with the command of the 9th Corps, that he went to Kostajnica to coordinate activities around Kostajnica and that he was arming the zone staff of the TO at Kordun. Can you continue -- and then I asked you how you knew that about with respect to those three points, and you started -- you started giving examples. Could you continue answering that question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As concerns the coordination at Kostajnica, I learned about that in relation to the events of arresting or detaining Mr. Martic at Otoka, close to Bosanska Krupa in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That took place between the 8th and the 9th of September 1991 and, of course, after he returned from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We are going to talk about that subject at length later in your testimony but maybe you could just tell us, who arrested Mr. Martic at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unclear whether he was arrested or whether he was just provisionally kept at the police station to be protected from the masses who gathered in front of the police station, and he was kept inside the police station in Bosanska Krupa in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How long was he kept?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two, perhaps one day, one night, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: As I said we will talk about that more later in your testimony. But how did you learn about the coordination at Kostajnica through those events? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he went together with Colonel Smiljanic who was the head of security of the 10th Zagreb Corps in the region of Kostajnica to coordinate combat activities in relation to the liberation of Kostajnica. That was the explanation as to why he went up there with Smiljanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who gave you that explanation? How did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I heard that in my telephone conversations with Radovan Karadzic, and then with Martic's aide, Nikola Omanovic, and then, of course, after Mr. Martic returned, and I heard that from some other people that I had contacts with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Nikola Omanovic, who was he? You identified him as Martic's aide. Can you give any more information about who he was, what role he played at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an employee with the Knin police station. By profession I believe he was a fireman and a policeman, and he was one of the two Martic's aides from the very start, from the signing of the petition back in 1990 and throughout the events. At that time, he was Martic's aide in charge of public safety, of sorts, but he was a very close person to Martic. He also managed the training centre at Golubic. He was in charge of administration there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, finally, you said that you knew that Mr. Martic was arming the zone staff of the TO at Kordun. Could you tell us how you knew that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that information from the Commander of Staff, Mile Bakic. I met him when -- as he was transporting a truck of weapons from Martic to Petrova Gora, sometime in August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that Mile Bakic or Mile Dakic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dakic, with a D.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did that meeting occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was by chance. We met on the road, between Bosanska Krupa and Bosanski Novi, closer to Bosanski Novi, and close to the Ada, which is a motel, in front of a bar, a cafe, and that is in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who -- do you know who owned that bar or cafe?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. That was outside of the town, a small cafe. It wasn't in Bosanski Novi itself in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you learn when you met Mile Dakic? What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him what he was doing there. I was on my way back from Belgrade and I stopped by at Bosanski Novi to go to Mile Grbic's restaurant. On my way to Knin, as I came out of Novi, I saw the truck, I stopped because I saw him standing by the truck, and I asked him what he was doing there and he said, "Well I'm transporting a truck of weapons sent by Martic." I asked him where he was going to because I knew that the bridge at Bosanski Novi was controlled by the Bosnia-Herzegovina police. He explained to me that there was another bridge, an old wooden bridge, prior to Bosanski Novi, on the border between Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that there is no border check there. He could use that road to go via Glina and Topusko to reach Petrova Gora in the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Mile Dakic was -- did he hold any position or who was he at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the then commander of the zone staff of the TO for Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go back to an earlier answer that you gave when I -- when I asked you if, as a result of these decisions at the beginning of August 1991 you were able to get control over the TO, you responded that you were not and you gave two reasons. You said Milosevic said that Martic should be commander of the TO, you've explained that. And because of the influence of the JNA and the Secretariat for National Defence. Do you have anything to add to that second part of the answer, any explanation about the influence of the JNA that prevented you from gaining control over the TO at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list of military recruits and all the affairs concerning national defence fall under the jurisdiction of the Secretariat of National Defence and its offices in various municipalities. According to the federal law these offices have to contact federal authorities when such questions arise. Both the municipal and the republican level had to contact the federal level. Another obligation they had was to keep their list of people to be mobilised in case of need and to coordinate with the JNA units in the field. That is in their area, concerning the so-called organisational mobilisation issues. And often, such offices could not have functioned or could not do anything in relation to a recruitment or mobilisation prior to them coordinating with the JNA units or with the higher instance of the Secretariat. The other way was that certain municipalities were under the influence of the League of Communists and in particular the movement for Yugoslavia which was the military wing, and as it happened in the field, many people elected were the prominent people who would then have to choose whether they would organise police units or the TO units, depending on whose influence was greater in a particular area, whether the state security or the army's, and that was the situation in the field in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, yesterday you testified that you had made a number of appointments to TO positions during the fall of 1991. Can you explain to us a little bit how those appointments were made? What was the process for those appointments being made?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those appointments first started being made slightly before the 1st of August, and it went on throughout August and September for the most part in 1991. After this initiative concerning the setting up of the united system of Territorial Defence within SAO Krajina, I issued a number of decrees and I made several political appointments. I appointed people who I thought embraced the political concept of the system, such as Dr. Jovic or Mile Dakic who was the president of the Independent Yugoslav Democratic Party and some other people, but because of the conflicts that I referred to earlier and because of the resistance put up by the volunteer groups and the 7th Banija division at Banija and because of the resistance from the JNA, these people could exert no influence, and finally I started receiving proposals for the General Staff of the JNA and from Milosevic himself regarding further appointments and that happened by the end of September 1991, and that is when the system as such started functioning, as soon as I started signing the appointments for people who had been sent from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How would that happen specifically? Concretely, specifically? That is, how would you receive these proposals from the General Staff of the JNA and from Milosevic himself?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from Milosevic himself. I mean, I explained that how we started talking about it, at the meeting that Mr. Martic attended as well. I said that Territorial Defence could only be led by an expert military person, such as an army general or somebody else from the army, and that's when the whole story started regarding the setting up of the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence for SAO Krajina. Milosevic dragged his feet a little bit but then in the end he promised his assistance. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have a further meeting with Mr. Milosevic concerning the setting up of a Main Staff of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him at least once in the beginning of September, perhaps it was the 6th or the 7th of September I can't recall the exact date now and I was also in touch with him once again by the end of September, and I was also in touch with the Serbian Defence Ministry, through Minister Simovic in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In these meetings with Mr. Milosevic in September, can you tell us what was discussed concerning the setting up of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he would send people for the Main Staff. Since one person put their name forward already, he volunteered, it was a colonel from the command of the defence of the city of Belgrade, who presumably had some military training, and he had all the preconditions to be made general. So he was one of the candidates plus some other people. And Milosevic said that they would send these people down. That was his decision at the time. But time went by, it all lasted for a while, two weeks went by and I called him up and I asked about the staff and he said they are on their way. They will be there tomorrow. But basically, yes, in a couple of days they did arrive. Some officers from the General Staff from Belgrade and they said that they had an order from the General Staff for them to become members of the Main Staff of the TO of the SAO Krajina and I asked who the commander was, whether it was Colonel Maksic who came down with them as well, and they said, no, you should get in touch with Minister Simovic and he'll explain everything. He was the Defence Minister of Serbia at the time. And I called him on the phone from the office of the then command of the Main Staff. It was Martic's office, in fact, within the fortress and he was present there and everybody was waiting to hear what Simovic was going to say and Simovic said we have decided that the commander should be Ilija Djuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, I want you to explain something because you testified earlier that you had a meeting with Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Martic in which Mr. Milosevic pressured you to appoint Mr. Martic to be the commander of the TO. And you testified that you didn't do that but now here in September, Mr. Milosevic is agreeing to help you set up a Main Staff of the TO. How did that occur? How did that -- what changed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an essential change, in fact. The JNA became an active participant in the war, the JNA went to war and under such conditions all TO units automatically came under the command of the JNA, so that he had no further problems about this command issue, with regard to that particular line of command, through the JNA and the TO, and according to my assessment he must have decided that it was no problem and therefore the command should go through the JNA and not the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen, that the JNA became an active participant in the war? When did that change occur?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the end of August 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there a specific event?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An attack at Kijevo in the municipality of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When the General Staff was created at the end of September 1991, did that give you any power over the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Main Staff came under the command of the 9 corps and the zone staff for Kordun and Banija was under the command of the 2nd operational or rather the command of the 2nd Operational Group or zone of the JNA, which was located at Simajic [phoen] under the command of General Spiro Nikovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now moving ahead in time to October of 1991, did you have a meeting with General Vukovic of the 9th Corps concerning the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With regard to the positions of the TO, supplies, funding, command and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff of TO, General Ilija Djuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember seeing anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, was General Vukovic there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Djuic and myself went to see General Vukovic. That's the meeting we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was there any discussion at that meeting about the command of the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was about who would be in command and whether there would be an independent command for the Main Staff or whether they would have to follow the instructions by the Knin Corps, and I was told to go to Belgrade to see General Adzic and to get in touch with him. And General Vukovic said that he did not have the remit to decide these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you go see General Adzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What position did he hold at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the chief of the General Staff, the Main Staff, of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what happened in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told him about problems referring to supplies for the TO and the line of command for the TO and he said that the TO would have to be subordinated to the JNA and that there would be no changes there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit 167, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It's an information document. It is a report on the state of affairs within the Territorial Defence of the SAO Krajina dated the 10th of October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could look at the last page, could we scroll down to the bottom, please? Who is it from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From me. In other words, it was prepared by the people from the TO Main Staff and I forwarded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who did you forward it to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forwarded it to Belgrade, to Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you provide it to him in this meeting that you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was sent from the Main Staff of the TO SAO Krajina to Belgrade and I did actually discuss the report with Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. If I could just draw your attention to point 4 there, and if you could read that, please?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That the JNA and TO unit powers had to be delimited clearly, and especially with regard to the military involvement."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does it relate to what you were just telling us about, discussions about who would have -- how the command would function over the TO?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 190, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, after the RSK was formed at the end of 1991, what position did Milan Martic have?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of December 1991, Martic was the Minister of the Interior within the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was he at some point formally appointed to that position again when the RSK was formed, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In January, February, or rather in February, there were all sorts of combinations and things being discussed. There were conflicts about the previous government, the forming of the new government, but Mr. Martic on the 26th of February, presumably was reappointed as the Minister of the Interior at Borovo Selo, within the new government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look --

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or, rather, probably there was a decision about the Matkovic list on the 19th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at document 1860, 65 ter 1860, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, could we just establish, 26th of February of which year, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you see the document and do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a decision on the basis of which Mr. Martic was appointed minister within the government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina. It was dated the 25th of February 1992, and that's the time when I was not in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be marked, given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 191, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And until when did he hold that position within the RSK government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Governments changed. There was Zdravko Zecevic's, then Bijegovic's [phoen] Government, but he seemed to always remain in his post until the beginning of 1994, when he was elected president of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say that the governments changed, what -- and you gave several names, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring several governments of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, after the 26th of February 1992, or rather on that day, Zdravko Zecevic's government was appointed. Zdravko Zecevic was the president of the municipality of Benkovac and he became the head of the new government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina, and that government stayed in office for about a year until the beginning of 1993, and then Zdravko Zecevic handed in his resignation and Djordje Bijegovic [phoen] was appointed as head of government of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And your testimony is that during that time, during those various governments, Milan Martic remained as Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to go back, back to the beginning, back to the fall of 1990 and I want to talk to you now about issues related to financing, and financial support. In your 89(F) statement, your signed statement, you said that after the so-called log revolution, Croatia cut off funding or money to some of the municipalities that were involved in that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before the witness answers, talking about the 89(F) statement, there is a little point hanging about that statement. Maybe we could resolve that before we carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I raised that with Defence counsel at the break and he told me that he wanted to send me something in writing about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's between the two of you, but he also owes the Chamber an explanation. Mr. Milovancevic, you objected to this statement being handed into evidence yesterday, although it had already been handed into evidence, because you wanted to check whether it is identical with the statement that had already been admitted into evidence. Have you done so and what's your reaction to that statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The main point of the objection, Your Honours, was that the OTP tendered into evidence a signed statement which we did not have. In the meantime, we read the statement and we noticed four discrepancies in the text. We shall write a brief letter to our learned friend and I believe he will receive it tomorrow morning. I think this is a matter that can easily be settled between the Prosecution and the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, therefore, that -- the Prosecution can go ahead and ask the witness questions on that statement, because you will solve the problem --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for the clarification of the Court, I think that it's my understanding that those so-called discrepancies may be just corrections of typos, is my understanding, but we stand by our position that the statement is the same. But we'll resolve that between ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, the question that I'd asked you was do you recall stating in that statement that as a result of the so-called log revolution, Croatia cut off funding to some municipalities that were involved?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. Those were funds, additional funds, intended for the municipalities provided from the republican budget, to add to the funding of the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What, if anything, did those municipalities do to compensate for --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, I thought there was perhaps a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what if anything did those municipalities do to compensate for those funds that were cut off?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipalities stopped paying funds into the republican budget. They stopped paying the equivalent to the complementary funding they had previously received from the republic. The funds were collected on the territories of the municipalities so it was possible to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did this action of stopping to pay funds into the republican budget compensate for what had been cut off in the other direction or did those municipalities have to seek funding from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not enough. These municipalities were not very well developed, and with the escalation of tensions and the cutting off of communications, the economy became stagnated and began to wither away gradually. Assistance was sought in Belgrade, from Serbia; that's to say from Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was that done?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
