utterances.text: It was done in several ways. Assistance was sought directly from Milosevic asking him to provide funds for certain companies and institutions. Certain ministries of the Republic of Serbia also helped certain ministries or structures in the Krajina. Municipalities in the Krajina found sponsors among Serbian municipalities. Companies found sponsors in Serbia. These were always in which funds were channelled from Serbia and the Krajina became completely dependent in economic and monetary terms on Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which ministries from the Republic of Serbia helped ministries or structures in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of the Interior, the Ministry of Energy, the Ministry of Health.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting in December of 1990 with Mr. Milosevic concerning a factory in Knin?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The director of the factory asked me to ask Milosevic for assistance. He wanted Milosevic to help pay the debt of the nut and bolt factory in Knin. It owed money to the Split Bank, amounting to some 48 million dinars and the factory was actually facing bankruptcy because of this debt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the name of the factory?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tvornica Vijaka Knin, TVK for short.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you meet with Mr. Milosevic on this subject?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I told him this and I asked for his help. He promised he would solve the problem. He promised to help us and provide the money.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how he did that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell us, but I assumed how this was done. Ante Markovic, the then Prime Minister, announced that Serbia had intervened in the payment system of Serbia and pulled out a large amount of money.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Yugoslavia, not Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that announcement made?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was either at the end of 1990 or the beginning of 1991. I don't recall the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did the accounting system in the Krajina work at that time, at the end of 1990, beginning of 1991? That is for public structures.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In all of former Yugoslavia and in all the republics, there was a unified accounting system through which payments were made. As tensions between the Krajina and Croatia escalated, Croatia interrupted payments with Krajina, and payments in May 1991 between the Krajina and Croatia had been cut off, interrupted, and the same happened with respect to the entire accounting system of Yugoslavia. At that time, payments were made in the following way. Companies, municipalities and various organisations opened their accounts, not where they had their headquarters but rather in Belgrade. They would then go to Belgrade carrying cash or taking cash from there. The system was mainly for people to go to Belgrade and take cash from those accounts, carrying it to the Krajina, and to make cash payments. This situation obtained until May 1992, when the Social Accountancy Service was established in Krajina and it linked up with the same service in Belgrade. In this way, the payment system in the Krajina was set up through the same kind of payment system in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear, when you said that before May of 1992, companies, municipalities and various organisations opened accounts in Belgrade and carried cash, are you referring -- are those companies, municipalities, and organisations in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I have to say there is an error. I may have made an error. Until May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That's right. Until May 1991. Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can. Just to be clear, when you said that before May of 1991, companies, municipalities, and various organisations opened accounts in Belgrade and carried cash, are you referring to companies, municipalities, and organisations in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the regulations that had been in force until then, they had to have accounts in their own municipalities. However, they opened so-called non-residential accounts on a territory which was not their home territory. So instead of opening accounts at home, they opened accounts in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I forgot to ask you a question about the nut and bolt factory, TVK. Did that factory have any military function then or later?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a small scale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what it did?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The factory produced a kind of bomb. It was called a Tikusa [phoen]. The factory supplied some of the materials needed for Frenki's armoured vehicle pool.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that? When did it do those things?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of April 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did -- the SAO Krajina was created at the end of 1990. Did it -- did it at some time have a formal budget?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Krajina established or set up its budget after the government was set up on the 29th of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where did the money come from for that budget?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The budget was very impoverished. It was practically non-existent. Initially, funds for the budget arrived from revenue collected in the municipalities in the Krajina. Later on, it was funds from Belgrade or Serbia that flowed into the budget.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was the police in the SAO Krajina financed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was mainly financed with funds and materiel coming through the Serbian State Security Service and Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the general rule, as it was in the case of other ministries. The information about the funds coming from the state security of Serbia for the Golubic camp was something I personally heard from Jovica Stanisic who was the chief of the state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did he tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that in August 1991, after Captain Dragan had left Knin, after he had been withdrawn. He told me that he had been given a large amount of money for the camp and that they were now looking for him to get the money back, as he hadn't spent it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: At the government session in July of 1991, did Milan Martic talk about funding or funding of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had very big demands for funds for the police. The government of the Krajina was unable to meet these demands. There was very little money in the budget for all kinds of needs that had to be funded from the budget. Mr. Martic, in agreement with the then Minister of Finance, Bauk, used all the funds in the budget which had been earmarked for either things but even that was not enough. So at a government session, he asked for more. We told him there wasn't any more. And he then said that he would work for the one who was paying him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did you understand him to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he would work for the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us how the TO was financed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence was financed through the JNA and through the giro account into which funds were paid from the ministry and the government of Serbia, through certain technical channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which ministry?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 211, which is also Exhibit 41 in evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the next-to-last page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have asked you what it is.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to read out the correct title? Can you show me the front page, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go back to the front page, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a request for necessary ammunition and other military equipment. Addressed to the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia, to Lieutenant General Tomislav Simovic personally, and the date is the 18th of September 1991. The needs mentioned are the needs of the Serbian Autonomous District of Krajina the Main Staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go to the next-to-last page, please? And scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on the right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's Mr. Martic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the stamp of the staff of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the name on the left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Savo Radulovic from the municipal TO Staff in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And tell us again who was Tomislav Simovic at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the then Defence Minister with the government of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why is this request for assistance coming from Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, he was in charge of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you aware of this request at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you yourself have meetings with Mr. Simovic, Tomislav Simovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did those occur and where?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several. We saw each other a couple of times in September of 1991 and then in November of 1991 in Belgrade at his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were those meetings about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During one of the initial meetings we discussed the organisation of the TO and the needs to finance and equip the TO. During the second meeting, we discussed the peacekeeping operation of the UN in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you speak to Tomislav Simovic, the Minister of Defence of Serbia, about these issues?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there were no finances in the Krajina. There was no equipment, no materiel, to equip the TO. And that was based on Milosevic's recommendation that I go and speak with Simovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did he make that recommendation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the discussions we had concerning the forming of the TO Staff in September or late August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know what the relationship was between Mr. Milosevic and the Ministry of Defence of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic controlled the government of Serbia and Simovic was one of the ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look please at 65 ter Exhibit 182?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise the letterhead and the stamp on this document? For the stamp, we'll have to scroll down, please.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Those are the stamps of the state authorities of Serbia, the Defence Ministry stamp and the letterhead of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document addressed to the government of Serbia, and information on assisting Serbian areas in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 192, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 183, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, can you see what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document of the Ministry of Defence of Serbia addressed to the government of Serbia. This is information on providing assistance to Serbian districts in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the second page of the document, please? That is the second page in B/C/S and the third page on the English. And if we could scroll down on the B/C/S, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recognise the signature but it says that it is signed for Lieutenant General Tomislav Simovic. If I can read the signature properly, I believe it says Kuzmanovic. It was probably one of his aides.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Looking back to the first page of the document -- I'm sorry, back, I'm sorry, back to that page, that second page, did -- just one question I needed to ask. Do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the stamp of the Defence Ministry of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could go back to the first page, please? I'm just going to read the beginning. I think it's easier if I read it for the purposes of the interpretation. "Assistance has already been provided to the Serbs in Croatia but there is still an urgent need as well as numerous requests and demands for assistance in material supplies and equipment falling under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Serbia and for financial resources from the republican budget and the national defence funds of municipalities." And it goes on. Is that consistent with what you knew at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the second page. Now, I'm looking at the second page in the English and I think it's on the second page -- I believe it's the beginning of the third paragraph there on the page that you're looking at, it says, "Since there are no legal grounds, that is providing assistance to meet these needs is not regulated by the law, we propose that these issues be legally regulated by an appropriate decree, especially in view of the fact that these needs are great and can be expected to grow." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the last paragraph. We couldn't see it in its entirety on the screen. Yes, that's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The budget of the Republic of Serbia is put into force based on the decision of the Serbian assembly. That was the legal basis to spend the budgetary resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so what does this mean that there is no legal grounds for providing assistance? What do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the financing and equipping of some structures in the SAO Krajina was done contrary to the existing law in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, looking at attachment 5 of this document, which is page 7 of the B/C/S, page 8 of the English, it gives -- it lists in that attachment figures for different number of personnel for the TOs in various regions. For example in the Knin operational zone, there are -- it's -- it lists 12.000 personnel, Lika 5.800, Kordun and Banija is 20.000. Are these figures accurate for that time period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. I can testify as to number 1, 2 and 3. That was the figure, around 30.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 193, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that the police in the SAO Krajina was financed through the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia and that the TO was financed in part by the JNA and the Ministry of the Defence of Serbia. What happened when the RSK was formed at the end of 1991, beginning of 1992, in terms of the funding of the police?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police kept on being financed the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 232, please? Could we scroll down to see the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this -- the signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mr. Martic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise the stamp?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the stamp of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, dated the 10th of February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 194, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want to read the end of it, it says "I would like to inform you that the amount of 38 million dinars is located in the Glina SDK. These funds were paid earlier for the benefit of the TO but since the largest part of the Defence, i.e., the defenders, was financed from the army budget, these funds have been lying unspent for quite some time now. Could you please exert your influence in order for these funds to be transferred to the giro account of the Ministry of the Interior of the RSK," and then it gives the number. "Greetings from your comrade, Milan." 14 Is that consistent with your understanding of how funding was occurring at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if we could just look at the front page who is this document to, this letter?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was addressed to the Minister of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia for Minister Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally before the break, when the SVK or the army of the RSK was created, how was it financed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, that was the official title, after the 18th of May 1992, is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Babic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was also financed through the grants from the Ministry of Defence and from the budget of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence of Serbia or the Ministry of Defence of the SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Defence of Serbia, as well as donations from Serbia given to the budget of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court will adjourn for 30 minutes. We'll come back at quarter to six. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to talk to you about a different topic, and that is about media. If we could focus on 1990-1991, how did the Serbian media report on the situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of 1991, the media campaign against Croatia really gathered momentum, and it was shown in the media that Croatia was basically preparing for the slaughter of the Serb population in Knin, as well as the JNA members and their families. In January 1991, as I said, these reports started appearing in the press and all that fell within the framework of the preparations for the disarming of the so-called, as they called them, Croatian paramilitary forces, and basically trying to organise a military coup in Croatia. This campaign obviously, since tensions increased and armed conflict started, this press campaign turned into a real war propaganda at the start of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there, in the Serb media, talk about history, about things that had occurred in history?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serb media, these reports appeared much earlier, especially in the course of 1990. There was a lot of talk about genocide perpetrated by the Ustasha regime of the independent state of Croatia against Serb people, and there were daily reports about that, about the suffering of the Serbs, the Jasenovac camp, and all that was mentioned in the same breath as the new Croatian government which was basically suspected of being prone to repeat that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what was said about the new Croatian government in this media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, there was talk about it being a nationalist government, an Ustasha-leaning government or Ustasha completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is that a reference to, Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ustashas are Nazis, Croats, in fact, who were a puppet government of Hitler's Third Reich on the territory of the then so-called independent state of Croatia. Nazi collaborators from Croatia in World War 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's a historic term from World War II?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the report -- where was this reporting coming from?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It started and for the most part, continued in Belgrade, in Serb media, the dailies and weeklies appearing in Belgrade, and TV reports as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was the reporting accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to the reminders of historic facts, certain accurate historical data were reported but then it was presented in a special journalistic manner and it was brought within the same context of the new Croatian government which was only an assumption, and at the time it was incorrect. Later on, in the course of the war, and especially in the beginning of 1991, things escalated so much and the entire Yugoslav general public was acquainted with the film about the Martin Spegelj, and apparently it was funded by the intelligence service of the JNA, the making of the film, I mean. Croatian ministers and the Croatian press, of course, denied the facts presented in that film and it was basically impossible to find out the truth. But for the most part the media exaggerated things, emphasised certain things too much, and after the start of the war, they published inaccurate reports, especially after the unrest around Pakrac in March 1991. There were lots of things which were totally inaccurate or blown out of proportion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was there any discussion in the media, the Serb media, about Serbs and Croats living together in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, there were references to fears of repeat performance of this genocide by the Croatian authorities. And in this way, they fed Serb fears of the new Croatian authorities and they made them want to somehow defend themselves from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to observe what effect this media that you've described had on the population, on the Serb population in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, there was distrust. Then it turned into fear. And afterwards, animosity towards the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What about towards the Croatian people? Did it have an effect on the Serbs' attitude or feelings about the Croatian people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Being reminded of historical events and possible fear of what might happen in the future, of course, increased this feeling of uncertainty and -- which turned into hatred in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I would like to ask a question at this point. Was the media that you're referring to an independent media or was it controlled in some way by the Republic or the Krajina? I'd like to find out that before you proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the most part, the press was under the control of the authorities in Belgrade, in much the same way as the state broadcasting company. There was a local radio station in Krajina, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the relationship of Slobodan Milosevic to the press in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milosevic was in control of the state media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did he control the state media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By appointing directors and editors of the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And how did he do that in -- what was the mechanism for him appointing directors and editors of the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the control exercised through the state bodies, the assembly and the government, and they were the ones who appointed people to those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know any specific examples of directors or editors who were appointed by Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. He himself used to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did he talk about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1991, after the events in Belgrade where people were protesting against RTV Belgrade and the director of that TV station, Mr. Mitevic. At the time I visited Milosevic in Belgrade and he said the following: "Here, I gave them a new director," and he gave me his name, I can't recall it now. "His father was a Ljotic man, supposedly they will be happy now." And I also heard about or rather from Zika Milic who was the editor of Politika, it was a daily newspaper, that it was Milosevic who kept him in his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with him in the period between 1990 and 1995, and he said that to me in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Babic, did you yourself participate in making extremist statements in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, initially. Initially, it was a bit toned down and then my tone became ever sharper as time went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1991 in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter Exhibit 48, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It is an article from Nin. It's an interviewer I gave to Stefan Grubac who was a journalist for that weekly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And where was Stefan Grubac based? Where did he work as a journalist?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade, at the Politika press agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe what your relationship was to Stefan Grubac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were fairly close. He was from the area around Knin by origin and he was a journalist in Belgrade and in mid-1991 we actually became friends. He often did interviews with me and sometimes he suggested what I should say, how I should come across, and what I should emphasise or stress or say and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you know what his relationship was to Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through his friends, he had contacts with the Milosevic family, through Snezana Aleksic, who was a close friend of the Milosevic and Markovic family. Actually, he was a member of Mrs. Markovic's party, and Mrs. Markovic was Mr. Milosevic's wife. And through her he even managed to get me Slobodan Milosevic's home telephone number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in March 1991, at the time of the protests and the time when I used to be called to Belgrade to support Milosevic in relation to those protests and about what I wrote in my declaration. Stevo Grubac suggested to me I should be more vocal against the opposition and he said to me, and these were his words, that "that way Milosevic will like it better."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, I want to go back to this article and if we could go to page 9 of the English and the last page of the B/C/S, I just want to ask you a couple of questions about this article. If you look --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could move it over so that the column on the right is fully visible, because it's cut off now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you look at the first question in the third column and the answer, and on the English it's about halfway down on page 9, there is -- in your answer, you refer to the Ustasha-oriented police leadership. As your tone, as you said, became sharper in the media, is this a term that you used, Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the term is Ustasha-oriented, not really Ustasha as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. But on other occasions did you use the term Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most often I opted for the other one, Ustasha-oriented, and occasionally I certainly used the term Ustasha, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now if we could turn to the next page in the English, stay on the same page in B/C/S, about halfway down the column on the B/C/S, in response to a question, you say, and this is midway down the page on the English, you say, "As for Slobodan Milosevic he is the president of all Serbs, not only those in Serbia, and he enjoys the support of all Serbs." Did you believe that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence and may it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 195, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, still on the subject of media -- it can be taken off the screen, we are done with it. Still on the subject of media, how did the media report on Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several time periods in which Mr. Martic used to appear in the media quite frequently. First of all in 1990, and then in April-May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, first tell us about 1990.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Martic was promoted as a Serb national hero in his statements in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was that in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Starting in July and August, after the uprising or rather the protests of the Knin police force and the so-called log revolution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in April -- you mentioned April and May of 1991. What happened then with regards to Mr. Martic and the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since April 1991, he started holding regular press conferences, together with his staff, at the Secretariat of the Interior of Krajina, and he would talk about the situation and the security situation in particular in the SAO Krajina. He would talk about the police actions with regard to disarming the arrests of Croatian police officers, the help that we were meant to be getting from Slobodan Milosevic in order to arm ourselves. So mostly about these topics. About the cooperation with the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What did he say about, if you recall, about disarming and arrests of Croatian police officers?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that they were being successful and that they had arrested several people and he mentioned the numbers, how many of those police officers they were holding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After that, was there any -- were there any other periods where Milan Martic was promoted in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was particularly promoted in September, about the detentions and arrests near Bosanska Krupa and Otocac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's September of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified at the beginning of today about a covert strategy and a public strategy that was followed by Mr. Milosevic with regards to the future of Yugoslavia and a state for all Serbs. Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What were Milan Martic's views on that subject?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He blindly followed Milosevic's policy or the policy of the service. He was a man of the service. That's what we can say about him. What was planned there and what was done there, he continued to do. He was a follower of the -- of Milosevic's security services. And he believed in Slobodan Milosevic as his leader and the leader of all Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He talked about it publicly and that was his opinion in private as well. Even after the elections in 1995, both before and after the elections and in the course of 1994 when he became president of the republic, he said that he was going to hand his powers over to Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On April 1, 1991, still on the subject of the covert strategy and the public strategy, the SAO Krajina issued a decision on annexing the SAO Krajina to Serbia, and this is part of your written statement.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Slobodan Milosevic react to that decision?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very forcefully, and he asked for it to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he say why?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that we had to speak out in favour of Yugoslavia, and that others should leave Yugoslavia but that this was something that shouldn't be stated publicly. That we were not supposed to be talking about our plans in public. Or rather he explained it in his own special way. He said more or less some academics are telling me that you need to be killed for the way you do things. That's how he explained it indirectly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was this reaction part of the strategy that you talked about before?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The action was in line with the arrival at a political goal that he himself had set for everyone, but not openly, not in the public domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the referendum that was held in the SAO Krajina in May of 1991, did you have any discussion with Mr. Milosevic about what the wording of the referendum should be?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked for the question for the referendum to be changed, and for us not to talk about annexation to Serbia but that we should vote in favour of remaining within Yugoslavia and following his intervention the question was indeed changed so that was the way we put the question to the public. "Do you wish us to remain in Yugoslavia together with Serbia and Montenegro and others who wish to maintain the state of Yugoslavia?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was this part of the same strategy?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified yesterday about the creation of the SDS in Bosnia-Herzegovina under Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 26, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a letter of congratulation from Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And who is it to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is he congratulating you for?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the proclamation of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was this sent?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 196, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you've spoken a number of times about a joint session that was held in Grahovo at the end of June of 1998. Can you explain what that session was about? Who was involved, what it was about? I'm sorry, June of 1991. My last case was about 1998. Can you explain what that session was about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a joint session of the assemblies of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina and the Association of Municipalities of Bosanska Krajina and it took place in Grahovo and there was a declaration there about the two parts being brought together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the reason for trying to bring these two entities together?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The political circumstances in Yugoslavia, the declaration of independence of Croatia and Slovenia. Those were the circumstances in which this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 90, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the declaration I was mentioning. Could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Subsequently was in an agreement on cooperation between the SAO Krajina and the association of Bosanska Krajina municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement on cooperation preceded this declaration by a few days. This was on the 27th, whereas the agreement on cooperation was adopted on the 24th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit number 85, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just understand one little point? Mr. Babic says this was on the 27th. I see it's dated the 12th of January or is it the date -- 27 is the date of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that if Your Honour looks at the document in its original, that date of 12 January 2002 is handwritten and I believe -- I can ask the witness what it refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, you see -- can we -- now it's been -- now it's not visible any more. Can we look at the date, the handwritten date in the upper right of the document? There. Mr. Babic -- we lost it again. There. Mr. Babic, do you see that and do you know what that refers to?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That refers to the year 2002, and these are my initials. This is probably when I handed the document over to the investigators of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that one of the dates that you participated in an interview with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you in fact give this document to the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now if we could go to number 85, 65 ter Exhibit 85, please. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the agreement on cooperation between the SAO Krajina and the association of Bosanska Krajina municipalities, which preceded the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would note that in the English translation there is a mistake in terms of the date. It says 24 July 1991, but it's evident on the original document that the date is 24 June 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We note your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was the substance of this agreement on cooperation? I'm not going to read through the whole thing but could you just tell us what the substance of it was?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substance was that there should be a link-up between the two regions, the SAO Krajina and Bosanska Krajina, that there should be integration in certain areas of public life, and social life. This would be the manner in which the Krajina would be linked up to the rest of Yugoslavia, according to the plans of Milosevic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was the Bosanska Krajina defined? What constituted the Bosanska Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the point in time when this agreement was signed, it was an association of municipalities in the Bosnian Krajina area where the Serbs were the majority population. They set themselves up as a region or as an association of municipalities and later they changed their name to the Autonomous Region of Bosanska Krajina. This was one of the so-called Serbian SAO regions which were formed during 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in connection with your preparation for this case and also in connection with your testimony in the Milosevic case, did you listen to some telephone intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you able to recognise some voices in those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you also able to identify the substance of what was being discussed in those intercepts or in some of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was able to identify the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the usher I would like to provide to the Chamber, we already provided this to the Defence, and to the witness, a bundle of intercepts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- with a declaration attached to the front which I will ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The tabs, Your Honours, with the numbers refer to the 65 ter Exhibit number of these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the bundle, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you look at the declaration that is on the front page there? Did you sign that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The declaration states that you listened to the attached intercepts and that you identified the voices and, for the benefit of the Chamber, the last column on the attached spread sheet indicates the voices that were identified by the witness. Is that true? Did you listen to those intercepts that are attached and identify those voices?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that the declaration be admitted into evidence, please. We are going to go through each of these intercepts and play portions of most of them. However, in order to save time I've done it this way. This is how it was done in the Milosevic case, in terms of the identification of the voices, and I'll ask further detail about it with respect to each intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the declaration will be admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number 199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Lost track of my binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you look at the exhibit -- the conversation that's marked 87? I believe it's the second one in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the bundle or in the first spread sheet?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. The bundle, please. There should be a tab that's marked 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you take a moment to look at the transcript of the conversation in your language?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in the bundle we have provided each intercept in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, according to the declaration you made, you recognised the voice of Radovan Karadzic when you listened to this conversation. Can you tell us, how many times did you meet Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More than ten times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to talk to him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to hear him speaking also in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, looking at this transcript, can you tell us what this conversation is about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an interview between Dr. Karadzic and a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play a portion of the transcript, and if all works well, we will be able on the screen to -- we will hear the intercept, obviously in the original language, and a transcript should play -- synchronised transcript should play on the screen as the conversation is being played. The portion that we are going to listen to starts on page 2 of the English transcript and it starts with where Radovan Karadzic says, "No, no," about halfway down the page. For the benefit of the witness and the Defence, it's page 4 of the B/C/S transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Mr. Babic, if you could look at page 4 of the B/C/S transcript, it's about halfway down the page on the B/C/S transcript. And if -- now I think that -- what do you have to -- is this computer evidence? On your monitor, to follow -- to follow the transcript being played, you have to press "computer evidence" which I don't know if that's already been pressed. And if we could play that intercept now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, what do you understand is being talked about in that portion of the transcript that was just played?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection. The Chamber exhibited the declaration in which Mr. Babic confirmed that he heard certain tapes and recognised certain voices. The questions put to him may relate to whether he recognises the voices on the tape or not. But as for the substance of the conversation, Mr. Babic can testify only if he was a participant in the conversation. For Mr. Babic to interpret what somebody else thought when they were speaking is unacceptable here. The issue at stake is one of the authenticity of the tapes but this will be established in the course of these proceedings. The fact that a voice is recognised doesn't necessarily mean that the conversation was held, in view of all the technical possibilities that are available. So I have now explained my objection, but the substance of the objection is that Mr. Babic cannot testify to what a person meant to say in a conversation in which he was not a participant himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question as put by the Prosecution to the witness was, Mr. Babic, what do you understand is being talked about in that portion of the transcript that was just played? Not what is meant. And if Mr. Babic does understand the language that is being spoken and is able to tell us what is being talked about, does he need, then, to -- that's not -- I don't see that being a question wanting to know what is meant. He can tell us what is said, can't he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect, Your Honours, I understand what you say, but we have all heard the transcript or seen the translation. Now Mr. Babic is asked to translate into his own words what the participants in the conversation were saying. It is, however, up to the Chamber to evaluate what the content of the conversation was. It's not up to Mr. Babic or even to my learned friend or myself. The Prosecutor can put something to Mr. Babic or ask him to confirm something, but for Mr. Babic now to interpret the substance of a conversation and his understanding of it, when he was not a participant in the conversation himself, falls outside the scope of his testimony. Such a question, Your Honours, could be put only if the other participant in the conversation was here and could be asked questions about what he actually meant to say. Mr. Babic's opinion here is irrelevant. What is important here is what the person speaking meant to say. This is only the personal opinion of a witness who was not a participant in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to Defence counsel, I think that it is just simply incorrect that an individual -- that a witness has to be a participant to a conversation in order to comment on it. Mr. Babic has already testified that he was there in -- involved in the events at the time, specifically involved in events that are being discussed in this transcript, and he has knowledge as a witness of those events, of these individuals, and of what is being talked about, and so he can give his understanding of what is being talked about and that can be of assistance to the Chamber in understanding this transcript. Your Honour is correct, I did not ask him what he meant or what he thought. That it would be going beyond what he could testify about, but he can shed light on this document -- this transcript by testifying to what he understood from his knowledge as a witness, from his participation in the events at the time, and really this is no different than any witness who comments on documents or articles or other things that are shown to them that they didn't themselves author but they have an understanding of because they were involved at the time. This has been -- this procedure is followed in every case of the Tribunal, and I think actually any case -- in any national jurisdiction this would be -- this kind of questioning would be permitted. There it was a second -- if I could address it, there was a second objection that was kind of mixed in with the first objection, which related to authenticity. It's not clear to me if Defence counsel is pressing that objection, but that's something that could be dealt with separately. But with respect to Mr. Babic's ability to comment on this -- on the transcript and on what is being said here and what he understands that to mean, of course he can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect to my learned friend, in my view Mr. Babic can give his explanation of the subject of the conversation only if it is not clear from the text itself. In this case, it's quite clear and evident. Mr. Babic is not an expert in constitutional law, he is not a legal expert, he is not an expert of any kind. If the Chamber and the Defence and the Prosecution needs an explanation of intentions, the OTP is trying now to ask the witness, based on a conversation, to comment on the intentions of a person talking to a journalist. Your Honours, it's up to all of us to determine this based on evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, while I'm listening very carefully to what you say, I would plead with you to make sure that at least you do represent the facts correctly. I haven't heard that the witness is being asked to comment on the intentions of the person talking to a journalist. What I heard Mr. Whiting to be saying is that he's asking Mr. Babic to tell the Chamber what he under -- what he understands the conversation to have been about, in the context of the history of the time. I don't think that has to do with the intentions of the participants in the discussions. Obviously, the literal meaning of what was being talked about, we will see in the translations. We will also -- we can also see what the witness's knowledge, if any, is about what was talked about, not the intentions of the parties. However, be that as it may, I've heard your response. I just want to confer with the rest of the members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, there has been now a bit of time and I don't know if you still have in mind the portion of the transcript that was played.

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer? It wasn't picked up. Do you have in mind the portion of the transcript that was played?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you understand is being talked about in that portion of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are talking about the concept by which the SAO Krajina was supposed to be a part of the future state, to be created in the territory of Yugoslavia, that this future state would encompass all Serbs. The concept was the following: Those who wanted to leave Yugoslavia, they could, but the territories such as the SAO Krajina, who wished to remain within Yugoslavia, they will do so in a passive way, so to speak. That was supposed to have been the explanation put before the international public, as well as the Yugoslav public, that this future rump Yugoslavia encompassing all Serbs is not being pursued actively by the SAO Krajina secession from Croatia but that rather Croatia seceded from Yugoslavia and that the SAO Krajina remains within the rump Yugoslavia and joins the Serb territories in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is what they discussed specifically in this part of their conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the public strategy that you talked about earlier in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this intercept that -- the exhibit be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The exhibit is admitted into evidence, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We haven't established the authenticity of this text. The witness recognised the voices. All the transcripts were made from such recordings without prior knowledge of the participants. Such recordings can be done only by a very specific legal procedure following a decision made by the president of the Supreme Court of a republic or any such highest judicial body of a republic. Hence, the question of authenticity remains. The voice was recognised, but whether this conversation really existed, whether it was done in this context, whether something has been omitted, that is something that we should pay attention to. And it is up to the Defence to point to those issues and the Chamber should decide. The Defence believes that this transcript can be marked for identification, but as to its authenticity, we have no such data at this time. Therefore, this witness, who recognised the voice, is not a legal expert or a technical expert who could provide explanation as to whether all this that we can hear on the recording points to its authenticity or whether something has been cut out or pieces added on to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence is actually mixing together two separate objections, as I understand it. The first is authenticity. The second is legality. With respect to authenticity, the Prosecution has on its witness list witnesses who will testify as to the authenticity of these intercepts. As to legality, that's a separate issue which could be litigated separately. That is what I understood him to refer to as to these -- there has to be a proper order for these intercepts to be obtained. And that is a legal issue which actually has been litigated already in the Tribunal, it can be litigated again here and we can deal with that issue separately. I have no objection to the document being marked for identification at this time and later when we have the witness come and authenticate it we will move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe that will then be the quicker -- the convenient way of doing it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then what is it that's going to be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What it is, is 65 ter Exhibit 88 and it's -- sorry, 87, and it's actually in e-court so the -- I think the Registry can just assign it a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, then, Exhibit 65 ter 87 is admitted for -- it's marked for identification, I'm sorry, and may it please be given an identification number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification, 200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But since the Defence is raising a question about authenticity, I will ask an additional question or two of the witness with respect to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, is what you heard and read in this conversation, is it consistent with your -- what you knew about Mr. Karadzic's positions at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there -- based on your knowledge of the events at the time, is there anything that causes you to question the authenticity of this intercept?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we now look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Whiting, before you go on, is it the entire 87 that is going in or the excerpt?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The entire 87, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, could you look at number 88? According to the declaration, with respect to this intercept, you identified the voices of Radovan Karadzic and Andjelko Grahovac. You've already told us about your knowledge of the voice of Radovan Karadzic. Who -- do you know who Andjelko Grahovac was at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andjelko Grahovac, that was his voice. He was the then president of the executive council of the Association of Municipalities of Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to meet him and talk with him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Approximately how many?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About a dozen, not less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you talk to him on the telephone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play -- or let me ask you, could you look at the conversation and are you able to tell us what this conversation is about, just generally what it's about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Karadzic states his position to Grahovac that we should work on the integration of the regions but that we should keep silent from the public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play a clip that starts on page 2 of the English transcript. It starts with Mr. Grahovac saying, "Milan Babic was supposed to come here today." In the B/C/S it's at the top of page 2. So if you could go to the top of page 2 and we'll play that clip now. [Check]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, in that except, Radovan Karadzic says, "You should make an integration but don't sign any contract on it." What did you -- what do you understand him to mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should put the concept into practice but we should keep it hidden from the public. That is, to integrate the Serb territories without the public knowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play a second clip that begins at the top of the page, page 4 of the English transcript, and the bottom of page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we play the second transcript, please, the second clip? We don't seem to have sound. Sometimes technology fails us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, do you see in the transcript where Mr. Karadzic says, "That is very important -- very dangerous because in that case, he can alert the international public and Serbs are creating big Serbia." Do you see that? On the English transcript it's on page 4, about a third of the way down the page, almost half the way down the page. Do you see that, Mr. Babic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you understand that to mean?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's what I discussed a minute ago. If the public were to know that the Serb territories were to be integrated, then the international public would be put on alert as to what was really going on, that is that the Serbs were in the process of creating greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be marked for identification, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 88 is marked for identification. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be marked for identification, 201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I neglected to ask the same questions about this conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this conversation consistent with what you knew to be the views of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Grahovac at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is there anything about what you've heard or read with respect to this conversation that causes you to doubt the authenticity of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MILAN BABIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court will adjourn until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Courtroom II, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it Courtroom II?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what I understand, but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I defer to superior knowledge. We shall go to Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: be reconvened on Friday, the 17th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
